slides.heading: Oral Lesson
bullets: “A rich man owns that house.” — *rich* is an adjective element modifying *man*.
“A man who is rich owns that house.” — the words *who is rich* modify *man*:  also an adjective element.
*who is rich* is a proposition:  subject *who*,  copula *is*,  predicate *rich*.
So the sentence contains two propositions:  “A man owns that house” and “who is rich.” The second is an adjective element modifying the subject of the first.
Such propositions are called *Clauses*.

slides.heading: The Clause
bullets: A Clause is a proposition used as an element of a sentence.
Like every proposition, it has its own subject and predicate.
Like the adjective *rich*, the clause *who is rich* limits the subject *man* — not any man, but a rich man.
The pronoun *who* is not only the subject of a proposition, but it also joins the modifying clause *who is rich* to the noun *man*, which it limits.

rows.sentence: A man who is rich owns that house.
rows.note: Declarative. The principal proposition on the main line; the modifying clause on its own line beneath, the dashed line joining the relative *who* to its antecedent *man*.

rows.sentence: We honor men who keep their word.
rows.note: Declarative. Two propositions:  “We honor men” and “who keep their word.” The modifying clause limits *men*, an objective element; within the clause, *who* is the subject.

slides.text: A Relative Pronoun is a word used to represent a preceding word or expression, to which it joins a modifying clause.
examples: The man **who** is rich owns that house.
The house **which** he bought is old.
I like a horse **that** is gentle.
The friend **whom** you trusted has gone.
Take such books **as** you need.  (*as*, after *such*, *many*, *same*)

slides.heading: The Antecedent & the Relative Clause
bullets: The word or expression a relative represents is its *Antecedent*:  “the boy who studies” — *boy*.
A Relative Clause is a clause introduced by a relative pronoun:  *who studies*.
It modifies the antecedent — an adjective element telling which boy.
*what* is equivalent to *that which*:  “Take **what** you need” = “Take **that which** you need.” Its antecedent is not expressed.
The suffixes *ever*, *so*, and *soever* are sometimes added:  “**Whoso** keepeth the law is a wise son.”  (*whoso* = *whoever* = *he who*)

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Relative Pronoun
slides.instruction: Point out the relative pronoun in each sentence.
items: Those who sow will reap.
He that hateth, dissembleth with his lips.
This is the house which my father bought.
I gave him all that I had.
Judge ye what I say.
He will do what is right.
A kind boy avoids doing whatever injures others.
Whoever studies will learn.

slides.heading: Practice — Clause & Antecedent
slides.instruction: Name the relative clause, then its antecedent.
items: I have a knife that has a white handle.
He who studies will learn.
You have many blessings which I cannot share.
Solomon, who was the son of David, built the temple.
The Lord chastens him whom he loves.
They that forsake the law praise the wicked.
answers: that has a white handle  →  knife
who was the son of David  →  Solomon

rows.sentence: The fish which you caught is a trout.
rows.note: Declarative. *fish* is the subject; *trout*, the predicate; *is*, the copula. *fish* is modified by *the* and the clause *which you caught*, both adjective elements. Within the clause, *which* is an objective element.

rows.sentence: I like a horse that is gentle.
rows.note: Declarative. *like* is modified by *horse*, an objective element, which is modified by *a* and the clause *that is gentle*, both adjective elements. Within the clause, *that* is the subject.

slides.heading: Practice — Clause to Adjective
slides.instruction: Change each relative clause to an adjective.
items: I have an apple that is rotten.
I like people that are honest.
Will you buy me a knife that has four blades?
A little boy who is lame came to our house.
answers: Will you buy me a four-bladed knife?
A lame little boy came to our house.

slides.heading: Practice — Adjective to Clause
slides.instruction: Change each adjective to a relative clause.
items: Industrious people always prosper.
A barking dog seldom bites.
He has some counterfeit money.
The moldy paper was burned.
answers: People who are industrious always prosper.
A dog that barks seldom bites.
He has some money which is counterfeit.
The paper which was moldy was burned.

slides.heading: Who, Which, or That?
bullets: *who* — for persons:  “the girl who sings.”
*which* — for animals and things without life:  “the dog which barked.”
*that* — for either:  “the man that spoke,”  “the house that stood.”
Caution IV — Do not use *which* to represent persons, or *who* or *whom* to represent animals or objects without life.

slides.heading: Practice — Supply the Relative
slides.instruction: Fill each blank with a relative pronoun.
items: Death lifts the veil ___ hides a brighter sphere.
Blest are the feasts ___ simple plenty crowns.
The man ___ paid the money was the cashier.
The message ___ was sent was received.
No one can tell ___ others may do.
The girl ___ sings is my sister.

slides.heading: Practice — Correct the Relative
slides.instruction: Each sentence misuses a relative pronoun. Correct it.
items: The man which you saw is my father.
I love all which speak the truth.
Was that your dog who was killed?
I saw the man which was here yesterday.
The horse whom he rode was lame.
The oak who stood by the gate has fallen.

slides.text: The Interrogative Pronouns are *who*, *whose*, *whom*, *which*, and *what*, when used in asking questions.

slides.heading: Analyze — Interrogative Pronouns
slides.intro: A question's first word is not always its subject — arrange it as a statement to find its elements.

rows.note: Interrogative. *You* is the subject; *can trust* the predicate, modified by *whom*, an objective element.  (You can trust *him*.)
Interrogative. The subject is *that man*; *who* stands in the predicate, asking for the notion the answer supplies.  (That man | is : John.)

slides.heading: Interrogative Adjectives
bullets: *which* and *what* are sometimes placed before nouns; they are then *Interrogative Adjectives*.
“Which road shall I take?” — *which* modifies *road*.
“What noise is that?” — *what* modifies *noise*.
*whose* is the possessive of *who* — a pronoun still, as *his* is in “his book”:  “Whose book is this?”

rows.note: Interrogative. *Which* is an interrogative adjective, slanting under *road* like any other adjective element.
Interrogative. *boy* is the subject, modified by *Which*, an interrogative adjective; *prize* is an objective element.

slides.heading: Practice — Find the Interrogative Pronoun
slides.instruction: Point out the interrogative pronoun in each sentence.
items: What did he say?
Who wrote that letter?
Which trots the fastest?
Whom did you call?
Whose house was burned?
To whom did you give it?
For whom is this gift?
Who discovered America?

slides.heading: Practice — Pronoun or Adjective?
slides.instruction: Is *which* or *what* an interrogative pronoun or an interrogative adjective?
items: Which of these is yours?
Which book do you want?
What man would do that?
What did you find?
Which is the way to town?
What time is it?

slides.heading: Incorrect Language — Caution I
bullets: Do not use *him*, *me*, or *her* as the subject or the predicate of a sentence.
As subject:  not “Him and me went,” but “**He** and **I** went.”
Not “Her and her sister sang,” but “**She** and her sister sang.”
Not “Tom and him left early,” but “Tom and **he** left early.”
As predicate — after the copula, the predicate is in the nominative, like the subject:  It | is : she.
Not “It is her,” but “It is **she**”;  not “That was him,” but “That was **he**.”

slides.heading: Objects Take Me, Him, Her
bullets: An objective element — after a verb, or after *to*, *for*, *with*, *between* — takes *me*, *him*, *her*, *us*, *them*.
Not “She invited Tom and I,” but “She invited Tom and **me**.”
Not “This gift is for you and I,” but “This gift is for you and **me**.”
Not “He sat with she and Ann,” but “He sat with **her** and Ann.”
To test, drop the other person:  “She invited (Tom and) ___” → “She invited **me**” — never “She invited I.”

slides.heading: Practice — I or Me? He or Him?
items: Tom and (I / me) went fishing.
The coach chose Ann and (I / me).
It was (he / him) at the door.
Keep this between you and (I / me).
Mother sent (he / him) and me to the store.
My sister and (he / him) are friends.
Are you coming with Sarah and (I / me)?
The winners were Paul and (I / me).

slides.heading: Incorrect Language — Cautions II & III
bullets: Caution II — Do not use improper forms of pronouns.
Not “He hurt *hisself*,” but “He hurt **himself**.”
Not “They fooled *theirselves*,” but “They fooled **themselves**.”
Caution III — *you* should precede *he*, *she*, or *they*; and *he*, *she*, or *they* should precede *I* or *we*.
Not “She and you sang,” but “**You** and **she** sang.”
Not “We and they won,” but “**They** and **we** won.”
Not “I and he walked,” but “**He** and **I** walked.”

slides.heading: Practice — Correct the Language
items: Him and me were in the boat.
It was me.
Me and the doctor were there.
Him and you were tardy.
The boys dressed theirselves.
He made the kite hisself.
You, and him, and me were boys together.
We and he will stay in at recess.

rows.label: Personal
rows.text: Represents a noun and shows its person. Each takes three cases.
rows.examples: I / my / me  ·  he / his / him  ·  they / their / them

rows.label: Possessive
rows.text: Stands alone for both the possessor and the thing possessed.

rows.label: Relative
rows.text: Represents a preceding word, to which it joins a modifying clause.
rows.examples: The man **who** is rich owns that house.

items: What are clauses?
What is a relative pronoun?
Name the relative pronouns.
What suffixes are sometimes added to relative pronouns?
What is an antecedent?
Define a relative clause.
What is an interrogative pronoun? Name them.
Which of these are sometimes used as interrogative adjectives?
answers: Propositions used as elements of a sentence.
A word used to represent a preceding word or expression, to which it joins a modifying clause.
The word or expression a relative pronoun represents.
A clause introduced by a relative pronoun.
A pronoun used in asking questions:  *who*, *whose*, *whom*, *which*, *what*.
